Respiratory Illness Disrupts Ecuador’s Construction Materials Industry

A sudden outbreak of a respiratory illness among workers in Ecuador’s construction materials industry is causing significant operational disruptions, with several major sites reporting staff shortages and temporary closures as health authorities intensify containment measures.

The outbreak, first identified last week at a concrete mixing facility near Guayaquil, has now been reported at multiple sites in the provinces of Guayas and Pichincha, according to the National Association of Construction Materials Producers (ANPMC). As of Tuesday, at least 18 production plants and distribution centers have confirmed clusters of respiratory illness among their workforce, prompting concern over supply chain stability.

“We are facing unprecedented absenteeism rates, with some plants operating at less than 60% staffing,” said Carla Herrera, spokesperson for the ANPMC. “This has led to production slowdowns, shipment delays, and in some cases, the temporary suspension of operations to prevent further spread.”

Local health authorities have not yet identified the precise cause of the illness, but symptoms reported include fever, persistent cough, and shortness of breath. The Ministry of Public Health has deployed epidemiological teams to affected sites and is advising companies to implement strict health protocols, including mandatory mask use and staggered shifts.

Industry analysts warn that the timing of the outbreak could exacerbate ongoing supply issues. “The construction materials sector was already experiencing logistical challenges due to recent heavy rains,” noted Andrés Muñoz, an industrial economist based in Quito. “This additional shock is likely to lead to shortages of key materials such as cement and rebar, potentially delaying infrastructure projects across the country.”

At Hormigonera Andina, a leading cement producer, over 40% of the workforce at its Quito facility is currently on sick leave. “We have reduced output to prioritize worker safety,” said operations manager Jorge Salinas. “Our priority is to maintain a safe environment while fulfilling existing contracts as best we can.”

Trade unions are urging employers to increase paid sick leave and improve workplace ventilation. “Workers must not be forced to choose between their health and their livelihood,” stated Luz María Castillo, secretary-general of the Federation of Construction Materials Workers.

The Ministry of Public Health is expected to release further guidance later this week. In the meantime, stakeholders across the sector are bracing for further disruptions as the outbreak continues to evolve.
